action_criteria.expected_evidence: Four chronic infarcts: right occipital (PCA, from the basilar tip), two right MCA cortical and one right internal border-zone; Fazekas 2, no microbleeds
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with SWI and assign each chronic infarct to its arterial territory, with the white matter grade and microbleed status
action_criteria.rationale: Territory assignment of the infarcts is what separates a carotid from a cardioembolic mechanism, and SWI informs the anticoagulation decision.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not stop at the first mechanism found: atrial fibrillation and a severe ipsilateral stenosis are both active, and treating one leaves the other untreated.
Do not continue aspirin alongside the new anticoagulant outside a defined peri-procedural plan.
Do not lower blood pressure aggressively while a severe stenosis with border-zone infarction remains untreated.
Do not withhold anticoagulation because of age, cognitive impairment or the planned carotid surgery.
Do not certify fitness to drive; the dense hemianopia is disqualifying independently of the cognition.
required_recommendations: Diagnose multi-infarct vascular dementia with two mechanisms by territory: cardioembolism from atrial fibrillation (right PCA infarct) and the symptomatic right carotid stenosis (right MCA cortical and internal border-zone infarcts) [VASCOG_2014].
Start a DOAC (e.g. apixaban 5 mg twice daily: no dose-reduction criterion met at 76 years, 83 kg, creatinine 1.27 mg/dL) and stop aspirin, which has no separate indication [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].

Refer the symptomatic 80-90% right internal carotid stenosis to the vascular team without delay for carotid endarterectomy, the last ipsilateral event being 5 months ago; endarterectomy is preferred over stenting at 76, and stenting would add antiplatelet therapy to the anticoagulant [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].

Until the stenosis is treated, lower blood pressure gradually and individually (154/86), avoiding systolic pressure below about 120 mmHg and orthostatic hypotension because of the border-zone infarct; then aim for below 130/80 mmHg [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].
Intensify lipid lowering to LDL below 70 mg/dL (92 mg/dL on atorvastatin 40 mg): atorvastatin 80 mg, adding ezetimibe if needed [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].
Individualise the HbA1c target to about below 8.0% (8.1% on metformin and empagliflozin) without agents that cause hypoglycaemia [ADA_2025_older_adults].
Arrange hemianopia and cognitive rehabilitation, confirm he does not drive, and review with his wife in 6-12 months.

avoided_actions.rationale: The episodes were lasting focal deficits, not transient or fluctuating events: EEG answers no question in this patient.
No parkinsonism, fluctuation, hallucinations or dream enactment: a dopamine transporter scan answers no question in this patient.
No core feature of Lewy body disease; cardiac sympathetic imaging answers no question in this patient.
A stepwise decline after three dated focal events is not the subacute multidomain syndrome that indicates paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalitis antibodies.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.

accepted: Vascular dementia — multi-infarct type with two coexisting mechanisms: cardioembolism from untreated atrial fibrillation and severe symptomatic right internal carotid stenosis with a haemodynamic component

differential.key_features: The atrial fibrillation is real and needs anticoagulation, but it cannot explain a right internal border-zone infarct, and a severe ipsilateral stenosis with right-predominant white matter change needs its own management
The severe right stenosis explains the right MCA and border-zone infarcts, but not the right occipital infarct in a PCA arising from the basilar tip, and atrial fibrillation is documented
Fazekas 2 change is present and asymmetric, following the stenosis; the cortical infarct load is the substrate
Stepwise course with three dateable events, cue-responsive recall and preserved hippocampi
The visual deficit is a dense structural hemianopia from a striate infarct, not a progressive higher-order visual failure

key_clinical_evidence: Finding one mechanism does not exclude another: a right internal border-zone infarct is haemodynamic, while a right PCA infarct with a non-fetal PCA lies outside the territory of the stenosed carotid
Territory assignment is the analytic tool: lesions downstream of the stenosed vessel belong to the stenosis, lesions in territories it does not supply belong to the embolic source

The two treatments interact (anticoagulation for the arrhythmia, endarterectomy for the stenosis), so the antithrombotic plan is made jointly, and endarterectomy avoids the antiplatelet therapy stenting would need
A border-zone infarct calls for cautious blood-pressure lowering until the stenosis is treated
The uninvestigated hemianopia two years ago was the first stroke in this sequence

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Sergio Bianchi is a 76-year-old retired lorry mechanic who attends with his wife. Two years ago he noticed he could not see to the left; he stopped driving and did not seek assessment. His wife dates the beginning of his cognitive decline to the same period. He then had two further episodes: one of muddled speech lasting a day about a year ago, and one of left hand clumsiness five months ago lasting two days. After each he was permanently worse. He now cannot manage tools he used professionally, has stopped reading because he loses the left side of the page, and forgets what he has been told unless the context is given. His pulse is irregular at the bedside, which he says he has been told about before but never investigated; his sister has atrial fibrillation. He also has a right carotid bruit noted at a vascular clinic for the bypass and never imaged. He has polyvascular disease, diabetes and a 45 pack-year smoking history. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment.
